title: Churches in Houses
aka: the church that meets in their house
lead: For their first two centuries Christians met in private homes, not in buildings set apart for worship. The New Testament names several hosts: Prisca and Aquila, Nympha, Philemon, and the mother of John Mark in Jerusalem. A house church joined a household of family, slaves and guests to a congregation, which shaped how the letters speak to masters and slaves, husbands and wives, hosts and guests.

sections.h: The houses named in the New Testament
sections.b: In Jerusalem believers met at the house of Mary the mother of John Mark (Acts 12:12) and broke bread in homes (Acts 2:46). Paul greets "the church that meets in their house" of Prisca and Aquila in Rome (Romans 16:5) and sends greetings from it at Ephesus (1 Corinthians 16:19). Colossians greets Nympha and the church at her house (Colossians 4:15), and Philemon is addressed to "the church that meets in your house" (Philemon 1:2).
sections.refs: Acts 2:46; Acts 12:12; Romans 16:5; 1 Corinthians 16:19; Colossians 4:15; Philemon 1:2

sections.b: Because a church met in a household, its members included the owner and his family, slaves of the house, and guests. The letter to Philemon shows what this could mean: it is addressed to the church in Philemon's house as well as to Philemon, so Paul's request about a slave of that house was read aloud before the gathering, and Paul asks that the slave be received as a brother (Philemon 1:2; Philemon 1:16).
